meta.blurb: Lena can't sleep, and tomorrow is a big day. Follow her as she learns how sleep really works, why it goes wrong, and which small changes you can make tonight to wake up feeling like yourself again.
meta.bible: Lena: an accountant in her thirties who lies awake at night, learns how sleep works and tries small changes over two weeks. Key terms: Melatonin, Adenosine, Caffeine, Alcohol, REM, Circadian, Microsleeps, Insomnia, Apnoea, CBT, Cognitive, Behavioural, Therapy, Thyroid, Lark, Larks, Owl, Owls, Celsius, Indigestion, Heartburn, Adolescence, Dependence. Facts: sleep comes in cycles of about ninety minutes with light sleep, deep sleep and REM (dream) sleep; deep sleep is longer early in the night and REM sleep toward morning; most adults do best on seven to nine hours, teenagers eight to ten, school-age children nine to twelve; the body clock runs on about twenty-four hours and is set mainly by light; melatonin rises in the evening dark; sleep pressure builds the longer we are awake, linked to adenosine; caffeine blocks adenosine and half may remain five or six hours later; alcohol fragments sleep; insomnia disorder means trouble sleeping at least three nights a week for three months and affecting the day; the usual first treatment is cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I). Voice and tone: warm, calm, practical and a little humorous. Nobody gets personal medical advice; the book gives general information and tells readers to see a doctor about their own health. This book is general information and is not medical advice.

B1B2: It is two in the morning, and Lena is wide awake again. She has a big day ahead, and she wants to understand why sleep will not come.
Every person sleeps, and so do cats, dogs, birds and many other animals. Since sleep is so common, scientists believe it does something very important for living things.
During sleep, the body repairs itself and the brain sorts through the day's memories. Scientists are still learning exactly how this works, but the benefits are clear.
Sleep is not one long, even state, but a pattern that changes all through the night. The pattern repeats in cycles of about ninety minutes, and each cycle has light sleep, deep sleep and dream sleep.
In light sleep, the body slows down, and a small noise can wake you easily. In deep sleep, the brain waves become slow and large, and it is much harder to wake up.
Dream sleep is also called REM sleep, after the quick eye movements that happen during it. The brain is very active, vivid dreams are common, and the muscles stay nearly still.
Early in the night, each cycle contains a lot of deep sleep and very little dreaming. Toward morning, the dream stages grow longer, which is why you often wake from a dream.
Most adults feel and function best with seven to nine hours of sleep. Some people need a little less and some a little more, so the best test is how you feel in the day.
Babies sleep for much of the day, and school-age children need about nine to twelve hours. Teenagers need about eight to ten hours, although many get far less.
Deep in the brain there is a body clock that runs on a cycle of about twenty-four hours. It tells you when to feel awake and when to feel sleepy.
The body clock is set mainly by light that enters the eyes. Bright light in the morning tells the brain that the day has begun, and darkness at night tells it to prepare for sleep.
When evening comes and the light fades, the brain releases a hormone called melatonin. It does not knock you out, but it tells the body that night has arrived.
Sleep pressure is the second system that helps to control when we fall asleep. The longer you stay awake, the more a chemical called adenosine builds up in the brain, and the sleepier you feel.
Good sleep happens when the body clock and sleep pressure agree with each other. If the clock says it is night and the pressure is high, you fall asleep easily and stay asleep.
Caffeine works by blocking the effects of adenosine, so you feel less sleepy. It stays in the body for hours, and half of it may still be there five or six hours later.
After a short night, most people find it harder to concentrate and to remember things. Mood suffers too, and small problems can seem much bigger than they really are.
Tiredness slows your reactions and can cause tiny sleeps, called microsleeps, that last a few seconds. Drowsy driving is a real danger, so if you feel sleepy at the wheel, stop somewhere safe.
Studies link years of short sleep with a higher chance of heart disease, diabetes and low mood. Poor sleep is probably not the only cause, but it appears to play a part.
One myth says that everybody needs exactly eight hours. Another says that you can fix a week of poor sleep with one long lie-in, but research suggests this only helps a little.
Some people are larks, who wake early and feel best in the morning. Others are owls, who feel most awake late in the evening, and part of this difference is inherited.
Lena's first step is to get up at the same time every day, even at the weekend. A steady wake-up time keeps the body clock on track, and the rest of the night follows.
Soon after waking, Lena goes outside for ten minutes of daylight. Even on a cloudy day, outdoor light is much brighter than the light inside a room.
People who are active during the day tend to fall asleep faster and sleep more deeply. Exercise very close to bedtime can keep some people awake, so most prefer the morning or afternoon.
Caffeine is found in coffee, tea, cola and chocolate, so Lena counts all of them. She keeps her last cup for the early afternoon, and some people who are sensitive need to stop even earlier.
Alcohol can make you feel drowsy, so many people use it to fall asleep. However, it breaks up sleep later in the night and often brings early waking and a poor rest.
A large, rich meal late at night can cause discomfort and make sleep light. Going to bed very hungry is no better, so a small snack is fine if you need one.
Sleep comes more easily in a bedroom that is cool, dark and quiet. Thick curtains, a slightly open window and earplugs can all help, and a cool room is better than a hot one.
If you work, eat or watch television in bed, the brain begins to link the bed with being awake. Try to keep the bed for sleep, and do the other things somewhere else.
Screens give out bright light, and the content on them can be exciting or upsetting. Try to put them away about an hour before bed, and charge your phone outside the bedroom.
A wind-down routine tells the body that the day is ending. Lena takes a warm shower, dims the lights and reads a few pages of a paper book every night.
Lying awake, many people go over their worries and tomorrow's tasks. Writing a short list earlier in the evening can help the mind to put it all down at bedtime.
Slow, easy breathing helps the body to relax in bed. Lena also tries a body scan, in which she moves her attention from her toes up to her head and lets each part go loose.
A short nap of about twenty minutes in the early afternoon can refresh you. Long naps, or naps late in the day, can make it harder to sleep at night.
Checking the clock every few minutes makes the worry about sleep much worse. Turn the clock away from the bed, because the exact time will not help you sleep.
If you have been awake for about twenty minutes, get up and go to another room. Do something calm in dim light, and go back to bed only when you feel sleepy.
Sleep is not something you can force, and trying hard often keeps you awake. Instead, aim for quiet rest, because simply lying calmly in the dark is still good for you.
Everyone has a bad night now and then, and the body copes with it well. Worrying about it only makes things worse, so stay calm and keep your usual routine.
Doctors speak of insomnia disorder when trouble sleeping happens at least three nights a week for three months. It also has to affect daytime life, for example by causing tiredness or low mood.
The usual first treatment for long-term insomnia is a talking therapy called CBT for insomnia. It teaches the habits and thought patterns that help sleep, and it works well for many people.
Sleeping pills can help for a short time, but they can cause side effects and are not a long-term answer. Melatonin supplements also vary from country to country, so ask a doctor or pharmacist first.

Sleep apnoea is a condition in which breathing repeatedly stops and starts during sleep. Loud snoring, gasping and heavy daytime sleepiness are warning signs, and a doctor can arrange tests and treatment.

Sleep problems can have many different causes, and not all of them are connected with habits. Restless legs, pain, breathing problems, low mood and some medicines can all disturb the night, so a doctor should look at a long-lasting problem.
Shift work and long flights upset the body clock, because they ask you to sleep when it expects daylight. Dark curtains, planned sleep times and well-timed light can all help you to adjust.
During the teenage years the body clock naturally moves later, so teens feel sleepy later at night. Early school starts clash with this, and many teenagers do not get the sleep they need.

As people get older, their sleep tends to become lighter, and they may wake more often. This is common, but older adults still need a good amount of rest, and ongoing problems should be checked by a doctor.
Babies wake often, so their parents' sleep is broken for months. This is normal, but it is hard, so share the nights if you can and ask for help.

Sleep trackers count your movement and heart rate to guess how you slept. They are fairly good at telling sleep from wakefulness, but less reliable for the stages, and some people end up worrying about the numbers.
After two weeks, Lena falls asleep faster and wakes up less often in the night. She still has a poor night now and then, but she knows exactly what to do.
Habits take weeks to settle, so be patient with yourself. Choose just two or three of the steps, practise them every day, and add more only when those feel natural.

This book has given general information about sleep, and science is still learning more about it. It is not medical advice, so please talk to a doctor if you have worries about your sleep or your health.
C1C2: At two in the morning, Lena lay staring at the ceiling, counting the minutes and growing more anxious with every one that passed. She had an important meeting in the morning, and the thought of facing it exhausted only made her wakefulness worse. She decided that this time she would learn how sleep truly works, and then try to put that knowledge to use.

People sleep, and so do dogs, birds, insects and even some of the smallest creatures that scientists have studied, though the shape of their sleep varies enormously. A habit so widespread, and so risky for an animal that cannot watch for predators, must be serving a vital purpose. Researchers are still debating exactly what all of that purpose is, but they agree that it is not optional.

While we sleep, the body repairs tissue and the brain seems to sort the day's experiences, storing some and letting others fade. The details of how this works remain an active area of research, and several explanations probably apply at once. What is beyond doubt is that people who are deprived of sleep think, feel and behave worse.

Sleep is not a single, even state but a pattern that repeats through the night in cycles lasting about ninety minutes, though the length varies from person to person and from night to night. Each cycle moves through light sleep, deep sleep and a stage in which most vivid dreaming happens. A typical night contains four or five of these cycles, so waking briefly between them is perfectly normal.

Light sleep is the doorway to the night, a stage in which the heart slows and the body relaxes but a sudden noise can still bring us back. Deep sleep is different, with large, slow waves of electrical activity across the brain and a body that is very hard to rouse. Many scientists think this is the stage in which the body does much of its physical repair.

REM sleep, named after the rapid eye movements that accompany it, is the stage in which the brain becomes almost as active as it is when we are awake. Vivid dreams are common, while the muscles are temporarily switched off so that we do not act out what we dream. Researchers link this stage with emotions and some kinds of memory, although the full story is still unfolding.

The cycles are not identical, for the early ones are rich in deep sleep and the later ones contain more and longer periods of dreaming. This is why cutting a night short by two hours takes a disproportionate bite out of the dream stages, which are concentrated near morning. It is also why people so often wake from a dream just as the alarm rings.

Most adults seem to function best on seven to nine hours of sleep each night, and regularly getting much less than that is linked with a number of problems. Individual needs vary, however, and a few people do well on slightly less or need slightly more. The most useful test is not a number on a chart but whether you feel alert and well through the day.

Babies spend most of the day asleep, and children of school age still need about nine to twelve hours, because growing bodies and busy young brains demand a great deal of rest. Teenagers need roughly eight to ten hours, although surveys suggest that many of them regularly get far fewer. Lena, who had always thought of sleep as something for children, began to see it as a basic need for every age.

Deep in the brain sits a tiny master clock which runs on a cycle of roughly twenty-four hours, known as the circadian rhythm. It nudges body temperature, hormones, hunger and alertness up and down on a regular schedule, and it is the reason we feel sleepy at similar times each evening. Even people shut away in caves without clocks or sunlight continue to follow a rhythm of about this length.

The master clock is reset each day mainly by light entering the eyes, and it is remarkably sensitive to it. Bright light in the morning tells the brain that the day has begun, while darkness in the evening tells it to prepare for sleep. A pale, dim indoor life, by contrast, sends confusing and contradictory signals to the brain in both directions.

As the light fades in the evening, the brain begins to release melatonin, a hormone that signals to the whole body that night has arrived. It does not force us to sleep, but it prepares the ground by lowering alertness and body temperature. Bright light in the evening can delay its release, which is one reason that late-night lighting can push bedtime later.

The second system is sleep pressure, which builds steadily while we are awake and is partly linked to a chemical called adenosine that gathers in the brain. By evening, after sixteen hours or so on our feet, the pressure is high and sleep comes more easily. A long sleep then clears it away, and the whole process begins again the next morning.

Good sleep happens when the two systems work in harmony, with the clock saying that it is night and the pressure to sleep running high. When they disagree, as when someone sleeps late in the afternoon and then goes to bed at ten, sleep becomes shallow and slow to arrive. Almost every piece of advice in this book is a way of bringing the two back into agreement.

Caffeine works by blocking the receptors on which adenosine acts, so the pressure to sleep is still there but we no longer feel it. The body clears it slowly, and about half of a cup of coffee may still be circulating five or six hours later, though people differ widely in how fast they process it. A late-afternoon coffee can therefore interfere with sleep that night, even if it seems to have no effect at the time.

After even a single short night, attention wanders, memory becomes patchy and the mood tends to darken, so that small irritations loom much larger than they deserve. Lena noticed that she snapped at colleagues and forgot names she usually knew well. Studies of people kept awake in laboratories show the same pattern, and it grows stronger the longer the sleep debt goes on.

Tiredness slows reaction time and can cause microsleeps, tiny lapses of a few seconds during which the brain simply switches off without warning. At motorway speeds, even four seconds covers more than a hundred metres, which is why drowsy driving causes so many serious accidents. If you feel your eyes closing at the wheel, pull over somewhere safe, and rest or take a short nap before you go on.

Large studies have linked years of regularly short sleep with higher risks of heart disease, type two diabetes, weight gain and depression, though in most cases the exact chain of cause and effect is still being worked out. Poor health can also disturb sleep, so the relationship between the two runs in both directions at once. Even so, the evidence is strong enough that doctors now treat good sleep as one of the pillars of health, alongside food and exercise.

There are several popular myths about sleep, such as the idea that everyone needs exactly eight hours or that older people need hardly any. Another holds that a long lie-in at the weekend can wipe out the debt from a short week, although research suggests that it repairs only part of the damage. A steadier pattern is almost always better than a cycle of shortage followed by a binge.

People differ in their natural timing, with some being larks who wake early and feel sharpest in the morning and others being owls who come alive late in the evening. Part of this difference is inherited, and it tends to shift with age, so a teenager's owl-like habits are not simply laziness. The aim is not to change your type completely but to work with it sensibly.

The first step that Lena chose was the one that sleep experts most often recommend, which is to get up at the same time every day, weekends included. A steady rising time anchors the body clock, so that sleepiness arrives at a predictable hour in the evening. It felt strange at first to set an alarm on a Saturday, but she told herself that it was an investment in the week to come.

Soon after waking, Lena stepped outside with her tea and let the daylight fall on her face for ten minutes or so. Even on a grey day, the light outdoors is many times brighter than anything indoors, which makes it a powerful signal to the body clock. Over the following days she found that she became sleepy a little earlier in the evening, exactly as the theory predicted.

Regular physical activity is one of the most dependable aids to sleep, helping people to fall asleep faster and to spend more time in deep sleep. Hard exercise late in the evening can leave some people wired for a while, so many do best with the morning or the afternoon. Even a brisk twenty-minute walk counts, and Lena began to take one every day after lunch.

Caffeine hides in more places than coffee, including tea, cola, energy drinks and even dark chocolate, so Lena learned to count them all. She kept her last cup for the early afternoon, and she noticed that falling asleep grew easier within a few days. People who are especially sensitive may need to stop earlier still, and it is worth experimenting to find your own cut-off.

Alcohol makes many people drowsy, which is why a nightcap has such a loyal following, but it is a poor bargain. As it wears off, it fragments sleep, suppresses dreaming in the first half of the night and often causes early waking with a dry mouth and a racing heart. Leaving a gap of a few hours between the last drink and bedtime helps, and cutting back helps more.

A large, rich or spicy meal shortly before bed can cause indigestion and heartburn, and the body's efforts to digest it may keep sleep shallow. Going to bed ravenously hungry is no better, and a small snack such as yoghurt, fruit or a slice of toast is perfectly reasonable. Most people sleep best when they finish their main meal two or three hours before bedtime.

The bedroom should be cool, dark and quiet, because the body temperature falls as we drift off, and warmth, light and noise all work against that process. Thick curtains or an eye mask can block out streetlight, and earplugs or a gentle fan can cover noise. Experts often suggest a temperature of around sixteen to eighteen degrees Celsius, though comfort matters more than the exact number.

The brain learns by association, and if the bed is where we answer emails, eat dinner and scroll through bad news, it comes to mean alertness instead of rest. Lena moved her laptop out of the bedroom and kept the bed for sleeping and little else. After a week or two, simply lying down began to feel like a signal that she could let go.

Screens give out bright, blue-rich light that may delay the release of melatonin, and the content they carry, from work messages to dramatic news, can keep the mind busy long after the light is off. Putting them away about an hour before bed removes both of these problems at once, and it costs nothing at all. If you must use a device, a lower brightness helps a little, though the change in what you are thinking about matters at least as much.

A regular wind-down routine acts like a runway, giving the body time to slow down gently before it must leave the ground. Lena began to take a warm shower, dim the lights, stretch for a few minutes and read a few pages of an undemanding paper book each night. The details did not matter as much as doing the same calm things in the same order.

At night the mind loves to rehearse tomorrow's tasks and last week's mistakes, and the darkness makes every item seem heavier. Lena began to write a short list of tomorrow's jobs and any lingering worries in the early evening, and then close the notebook with a firm click. The notebook, she told herself, was now holding the problems, and she could safely leave them there until morning.

In bed, slow breathing with a long out-breath helps the body to settle, and so does a body scan, in which you move your attention gradually from the toes to the top of the head. At each point along the way you notice any tension that you find there, and you let it soften. Neither technique is a magic key, but practised regularly they give the mind something gentle to do instead of worrying.

A short nap of twenty minutes or so in the early afternoon can restore alertness without much cost to the night, and many people find it invaluable. Long naps or late ones, however, drain the sleep pressure that you will need at bedtime. If you are struggling to fall asleep at night, it is sensible to skip naps altogether for a while.

Watching the clock turns every minute of wakefulness into a small piece of bad news, and the arithmetic of how little sleep remains only feeds the anxiety. Lena turned her clock to face the wall and left her phone in another room. Knowing the exact time, she realised, had never once helped her to fall asleep, and it had often done the opposite.

If you have been lying awake for what feels like twenty minutes, it is better to get up than to lie there growing frustrated, because the bed should not become a place of struggle. Sit in dim light and do something quiet, such as reading or listening to gentle music, and return only when your eyelids feel heavy. Lena found this the hardest rule to follow and, to her surprise, one of the most effective.

Sleep is an automatic process, like digestion, and the more anxiously we try to command it the more stubbornly it resists. A better aim is to let go of the goal and settle for quiet rest, since lying calmly in the dark is itself restoring. Paradoxically, the moment Lena stopped trying to fall asleep was usually the moment that she drifted off.

Everyone has an occasional bad night, and the body is far more resilient than the anxious mind believes, so a single poor night will not damage your health. What does cause harm is dread, because the fear of another sleepless night can keep us awake all by itself. After a rough night, the best response is to carry on as normal and go to bed at the usual time.

Doctors use the term chronic insomnia disorder when difficulty falling or staying asleep happens at least three nights a week for three months or longer, and when it affects daytime life through tiredness, poor concentration or low mood. It is common, affecting roughly one adult in ten at some point, and it is not a character flaw. If this sounds like you, it is worth seeing a doctor rather than struggling alone.

The treatment that most guidelines recommend first for long-term insomnia is cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia, often shortened to CBT-I, which teaches the habits and ways of thinking that support sleep. It can be delivered by a trained therapist, in a group or through a well-designed app, and many people see real improvement within a few weeks. Several of the steps in this book are borrowed from it, but a professional can tailor them to you.

Sleeping tablets can give short-term relief, but they carry side effects and a risk of dependence, and most are intended for use over days or weeks rather than months. Melatonin supplements are sold as medicine in some countries and as a food supplement in others, and the evidence for them is mixed outside a few particular conditions. Before taking either, speak to a doctor or pharmacist, who can check them against your health and other medicines.

Sleep apnoea is a condition in which the airway narrows or closes repeatedly during sleep, so that breathing stops and starts, and the sleeper is briefly roused many times without remembering it. Loud snoring, gasping or choking, a partner who notices pauses, and heavy sleepiness in the day are the usual warning signs. It is common, it is treatable and it deserves a visit to a doctor, since untreated apnoea is linked with serious health problems.

Poor sleep is sometimes a symptom of something else, such as restless legs, long-term pain, an overactive thyroid, depression or anxiety, or the side effects of a medicine. A doctor can look for these causes and treat them directly, which often solves the sleep problem at its root. This is one more reason why a problem that lasts for weeks deserves a proper check, rather than endless experiments with sleep tips.

Night shifts and long flights across time zones ask the body to sleep when its internal clock insists that it should be awake, and the result is the familiar fog of exhaustion. Blackout curtains, protected sleep times, short strategic naps and carefully timed bright light can all help the clock to adjust. Even so, long-term shift work is hard on the body, and workers should look after their health with regular check-ups.

During adolescence the body clock shifts later, so teenagers often feel wide awake at eleven at night and miserable at seven in the morning, and this is biology rather than bad character. Early school start times clash with the shift, and studies in some places have found that later starts improve both sleep and mood. Parents can help by encouraging morning light, regular hours and a screen-free hour before bed.

With age, sleep tends to become lighter and more broken, and the body clock often moves earlier, so that older people feel sleepy in the early evening and wake before dawn. These changes are common and are not necessarily a sign of illness, yet the need for rest does not vanish. Medicines, pain, worry and other conditions can add to the problem, and a doctor can help to sort out which of them is involved.

Babies wake often to feed and be comforted, so the sleep of new parents is inevitably broken for many months. It is normal and it does pass, but it is also exhausting, and a parent who is running on empty needs support. Sharing the night shifts, napping when the baby naps and accepting offers of help are all sensible, and any low mood should be mentioned to a doctor or nurse.

Wristbands, rings and phone apps estimate sleep from movement and heart rate, and while they are reasonably good at telling sleep from wakefulness, they are much less reliable at identifying the individual stages. For some people, the data is a useful and encouraging nudge towards more regular habits. For others it becomes a source of anxiety, and if the numbers are making you worry, you are allowed to take the device off.

After two weeks of small changes, Lena fell asleep more quickly, woke less often in the night and found that the morning no longer felt like a hill to be climbed. She still had the occasional poor night, but it no longer frightened her, because she understood what was happening and what to do. The meeting that had once kept her awake went well, and she felt alert from the first minute to the last.

New habits take weeks to settle, and the surest way to fail is to try to change everything on the first night. Choose two or three steps that suit your life, such as a fixed rising time and an earlier last coffee, and practise them until they feel natural. Then add another when you are ready, and treat each lapse as useful information rather than as a personal failure.

Lena switched off her bedside lamp, took a slow breath and let the quiet room settle around her, ready for whatever the night might bring. This book has offered general information only, and sleep science is still advancing, so it is not medical advice and cannot replace a doctor who knows you. If you are worried about your sleep, your breathing or your health, please speak to a medical professional, and then sleep well.
